   uncertain band (Noul 0.30 to 0.70, Choice top probability under 0.60) routed to a
   person, which took label agreement to 99.2% while still auto-deciding 74.2%.

## Where it fits what we run

Governance tier controls everything, because Jev is a cloud API and Baylor data rules
apply. **A** = no athlete or health data leaves the machine. **B** = possible only
after de-identification. **C** = blocked without IT approval.

| Cookbook / pattern | Our workflow | Primitive sketch | Tier | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `skill_suggestion` | Pick 1 skill from ~155 for each prompt | Choice over all skills + 3 Noul gates, then rerank top 3 | A | S |
| `classification_using_confidence` | Tag Zotero papers by topic; report a broader topic when unsure instead of dropping | 1 Choice over the taxonomy, back off one level below 0.9 confidence | A | S |
| `rerank_typesafe` | memsearch result quality | 1 Noul per query-candidate pair, sort by noul | A | S |
| `classifying_rag_passages` | Filter what reaches a prompt from memsearch or the vault | 4 Nouls: relevant, has evidence, contradicts premise, injection | A | M |
| `entity_alignment` | Athlete ID reconciliation across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, roster | 1 Score with 3 levels (different / curator / same) + 1 Noul per field | B | M |
| `composite-scoring` | Project registry ranking, prioritization slate | 1 Score per dimension, weights in code | A | S |
| `semantic_find` | Query the NCAA charter, policies, contracts by plain question | Choice over tagged line IDs + Noul "does an answer exist" | A | S |
| `citation_check` | Verify the Research in 5 deck and status report before sending | String-match the quote in code, then 1 Choice: supports / contradicts / says nothing | A | M |
| `sde_cascade` | Verify Claude's own extractions before they land in STATUS.md or the vault | 1 Noul per field framed so true means escalate, gate on max | A | M |
| `autoresearch_feature_discovery` | Turn free-text notes into numeric model features | Score + Noul per feature, answers become CatBoost columns | B/C | L |
| `function_calling` | Natural language to our own CLIs (`portfolio.py`, report commands) | 1 Choice over commands + 1 Choice per closed-set argument + a `stated` Noul | A | M |
| `hierarchical_classification` | Deep taxonomy walks (CPC-style research trees) | 1 Choice per level, beam search over probabilities | A | L |
| `llm_guardrails` | Screen anything scraped or pasted before an agent acts on it | Noul battery + severity Score, thresholds per policy | A | M |

## What this unlocks that we cannot do today

Four of these are genuinely new capability, not a cheaper version of something we have.

**1. Free text becomes model features.** The autoresearch cookbook turns 2,000 wine
tasting notes into 67 numeric columns and trains CatBoost on them. Held-out RMSE went
from 3.09 (predict the mean) to 2.47 (word counts) to 2.15 (just ask Jev for the score)
to **1.77** (38 decomposed feature questions). The decomposition beat asking directly,
which is the whole thesis. Our equivalent: coach notes, wellness comments, RTP
narrative, and scouting text become inputs to a model instead of prose nobody scores.
Start on CFB scouting or public text, which is tier A. Athlete narrative is tier B or C
and waits.

**2. Athlete ID reconciliation without a threshold to fit.** We have the same name
spelled four ways across Catapult, VALD, Perch, S2, and the roster, and today that is
hand-matching. The entity-alignment recipe makes the three Score levels *be* the three
actions (leave unlinked, send to a curator, merge), so there is no number to tune, and
rides three Nouls along in the same request to tell the curator which field disagrees.
On 450 pairs it settled 89% automatically and queued 11%. Athlete names are PII, so
this is tier B and needs a de-identified key mapping first.

**3. Ask a policy document a plain question.** Tag each line with an ID, send one
Choice over the line IDs plus one Noul asking whether the document answers at all. The
Noul is what stops it from confidently pointing at the closest wrong line: on a
question the GitHub ToS does not answer, the top line still scored 0.86 while `exists`
read 0.14. Point it at the NCAA charter, the Kitman and MyLink contracts, and Baylor
policy. Cap is 255 lines per request; longer documents need a two-stage narrowing.

**4. A cheap verifier in front of expensive output.** This is the one I would not have
predicted. Every deliverable that leaves this machine (status report, Research in 5
deck, evidence brief) can be screened per-claim before it goes out, at roughly $0.00005
a call. The sde_cascade rules for a good verifier signal: one narrow grounded yes/no
per field, framed so *true* means escalate, aggregated with `max` so one confident red
flag survives instead of being averaged into silence.

## Where not to use it

- **Numeric verification on its own.** Correcting my 09-19 chat answer: the citation
  pipeline does apply to the TOS brief, but the part that catches a misquoted number is
  the **code string-match in step 1**, not Jev. Jev's Choice catches "this section says
  the opposite of the claim" (it flagged one at 0.99 confidence). Use both, and do not
  ask Jev whether 3.2 equals 3.2.
- **Date and window arithmetic.** Kickoff-time math in the sleep scheduler, GPS pull
  windows, availability windows. Extract parts, compute in code.
- **Anything that needs prose out.** It does not generate. Output is free because there
  is none.
- **Any per-athlete GPS, force plate, DEXA, or S2 record**, until Baylor IT says
  otherwise. Our own smoke test already posted a hamstring-tightness note to
  `api.typesafe.ai`. It was synthetic, and it shows how small the slip is.
- **As a security boundary.** The injection Noul is a filter, not a gate. Treat every
  passage that reaches a prompt as untrusted regardless of its score.

## Sequence

**First: the skill router.** It pays off across all 23 projects rather than one, and the
fit question I flagged on 09-19 is now resolved: 182 skills render to 16,089 characters,
about 4k tokens, so our ~155 fit inside the 32k budget with room to spare. Measured on
488 requests against Haiku 4.5, wrong skill loads fell 16.8% to 7.3% and needless loads
9.8% to 4.0%. It fixed 37 requests and broke 7.

Design constraints that are not optional here:

- It runs as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which means a network call on **every** prompt.
  Our memsearch hook is currently failing with `ETIMEDOUT` 8x consecutively. Same
  fragility class.
- Therefore: hard timeout around 2 seconds, **fail open** (no suggestion, never a
  blocked prompt), and no retries in the hot path.
- Use the cookbook's exact wording, including "Ignore this if it does not fit what the
  user actually asked for." Pushing harder wins compliance on wrong suggestions too.
- Patch both `.claude/hooks/` and `.codex/hooks/`, and run it under the shell the
  MSYS-stall fix settled on, not Git Bash.

**Next two, in order:** Zotero backlog classification with confidence backoff (tier A,
small, and the 1,018-papers-for-$0.08 demo is literally the same job), then the
deliverable verifier on the status report and Research in 5.

## Corrections to the 2026-09-19 chat answer

Four things the full read changed:

1. The 32k fit question is answered: 155 skills fit comfortably.
2. Citation checking is **not** ruled out for the TOS brief. See above.
3. Fireflies renaming is workable as *selection*: code or an LLM proposes 3 to 5
   candidate titles, Jev picks one. It still cannot write a title, and it is still
   gated on stripping athlete names from the summary.
4. Memory deduplication is the entity-alignment shape (a 3-level Score whose levels are
   the actions), not a Noul with a threshold.

=== OPEN WORK ===
# Open work: the position-by-position screening matrix

This is deliverable 010. It was renumbered on 2026-09-15 (008 became the 2025
baseline load) and again on 2026-09-16 (009 became the workbook with the
Impact alerts). Draft it from the validation run,
`docs/2026-09-16-validation-run.md`, which measured worthwhile reviews and
overlooked players on 39 graded players. It was started on 2026-09-05 and never finished. Source criteria were gathered, approval was asked for, and the
session ended before anything was written.

## What it needs to be

A one-page decision matrix defining, per position, the minimum evidence that
earns a further look, which weaknesses are acceptable, and what the exception
paths are. Concrete proposed rules, not blanks for staff to fill in.

Label everything in it as proposed staff-review decisions, not as existing
workbook rules. The workbook's current thresholds are implemented but unproven.

## What Eric specified

- "Let's proceed with the first priority in the position-by-position matrix."
- "Propose minimums and exceptions for review."
- "There is also a role-mapping issue within the first gap: WR versus SLOT, END
  versus JACK, and CB versus STAR can have different requirements."
- "The thresholds haven't demonstrated recruiting usefulness yet."
- "Test known prospects, including players the filter misses. Measure both
  worthwhile reviews generated and worthwhile players overlooked, by position."
- "minimum thresholds for guys that are worth taking a further look at"

Do not collapse those roles into generic position groups.

## Role factors already in the workbook

| Role | Factors used |
|---|---|
| END | Strength at POA, Tackling, Block Destruction / Pass Rush |
| JACK | Pass Rush / Block Destruction, Tackling, Ability to Play in Space |
| CB | Man-to-Man Coverage, Transition Speed / Competitive Edge, Ball Skills |
| STAR | Man-to-Man Coverage, Tackling, Ball Skills |
| WR and SLOT | Shared core evaluation factors, separate size matrices |

## Telemetry to Baylor role mapping

- WR maps to WR, SLOT
- EDGE maps to END, JACK
- CB maps to CB, STAR
- SAF maps to SAF, STAR
- OB-LB maps to ILB, JACK
- C is graded on the OG/C tab

## Metric quirks to keep in mind

Traits and advanced stats are 0 to 100 percentiles against the same position
(FBS, 2019 to present). Exceptions: Top End Speed is raw mph, QB Risk Level is a
text label, Tackle Breaking is documented but absent from the portal grid, QB
decision-making surfaces as "Target Selection", DB coverage surfaces as
"EPA/Target".

Source: Codex session 01a0718d, 2026-09-05. The quoted lines above are Eric's
own words from that session. Everything else is drawn from the workbook and the
Drive folder's AGENTS.md.

=== MEETING ===
# 2026-09-15 meeting: potential Review Board changes

Source: Fireflies meeting `01M2K5PNEVK662KYQ74TK2DKWD`, "PP Recruiting: Review
Board walkthrough" (renamed 2026-09-15 from the default "Sep 15, 01:36 PM"),
51 minutes.
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01M2K5PNEVK662KYQ74TK2DKWD

## What kind of meeting this was

A working session, not a formal change review. Eric walked a player personnel
staff member through the 003 workbook's REVIEW BOARD. Fireflies did not name
speakers. Speaker 3 is Eric (he built the tool and sent the files). Speaker 1 is
the personnel staff member who scouts the portal. Other voices drop in and out.
Fireflies' own action-item attribution is unreliable, so the items below come
from the transcript, not its summary.

Everything below is a **request or open question**. Nothing was decided and no
workbook was changed.

Timestamps link to the recording: append `?t=<seconds>` to the URL above.

## Verdict from the room

The staff member's reaction was strongly positive. The REVIEW BOARD ordered by
projected band is what they want for pre-portal work: watch the players the data
puts at AA or AL first instead of watching by snap count. Eric's caution: validate
it internally before trusting it, and fix the missing and duplicate players first
(33:22, t=2002; 42:55, t=2575).

Target the staff member set: **30 to 50 names per position from FCS and Group of
6 schools, ready around week 5 or 6**, so they can spend the week or two before
the bye on pre-portal evals. The two-week window they named is this week and next,
before conference play (27:35, t=1655; 30:47, t=1847; 50:50, t=3050).

## Requested changes

### 1. Weekly refresh without hand pasting (priority, two-week deadline)

- Staff member asked for the easiest way to monitor this every week, and is happy
  to download and drop an Excel file each Monday or Tuesday once Telemetry updates
  (00:33, t=33; 25:14, t=1514).
- Eric's proposed design: raw Telemetry exports (likely CSV) go in a separate
  folder, Power Query loads them into PORTAL INPUT, formulas recalculate
  (24:25, t=1465).
- Cadence: weekly through the season. Useful signal needs two or three games and
  conference play, especially at lower levels (25:47, t=1547).

### 2. Pre-portal source: the Player Traits leaderboard, not the Transfer Portal

- For pre-portal, the source is the Player Traits leaderboard (FBS and FCS),
  plus Advanced Stats, not the portal view (15:13, t=913; 17:15, t=1035).
- Scope: FCS and Group of 6, "guys on the way up." Skip established Power 5
  producers (16:22, t=982).
- Staff member asked how the original portal load combined the Player Traits and
  Advanced Stats exports. Eric: there were about 30 working files behind the
  aggregate he sent (48:52, t=2932).

### 3. Leaderboard export does not match PORTAL INPUT

Tested live with a QB export (18:52 to 23:39, t=1132 to 1419):

- In the room: extra columns (committed-to fields and others), and Elig Yrs and
  jersey number looked missing. The later Telemetry check found both Elig. and #
  on the leaderboard views, so recheck against a real export.
- **Verified in the workbook today:** every REVIEW BOARD formula reads PORTAL
  INPUT by fixed position, not by header. Snaps is column H, player and QB traits
  are P:AI, advanced stats are AJ:BN, HT/WT are E/F. A paste with one column out
  of place silently corrupts every downstream flag.
- So the Drive `AGENTS.md` §6 line "column order need not match Telemetry but
  headers must" is wrong for the current formulas. The refresh (item 1) needs a
  header-to-column map.

### 4. QB trait coverage

QBs on the leaderboard have no Deep Speed and no change-of-direction or decel
values (23:17, t=1397). Effects in the current formulas:

- Speed alert still fires off Play Speed alone (it uses MAX of P and Q).
- ATHLETIC (data) uses CoD and Decel, so it goes blank for QBs. QBs can never
  reach 45 on "Critical 5 data pts".

content.text:
Confirmed — the Telemetry exports carry a stable `PlayerId`, and `load_leaderboard.py` already joins Player Traits to Advanced Stats on it. So the entity-resolution case I was going to pitch collapses into a code join. That kills the one I thought was strongest.

Here's the honest answer.

## Short version: not for the engine, and not yet for anything else

The screening engine is percentiles compared against thresholds — 75th percentile, 0.375 elite share, Impact ≥90. Jev's own jaggedness docs list counting, arithmetic, and comparing numeric representations as unreliable. You'd be paying a cloud round-trip to do worse what Excel already does for free. And your real weakness from the 09-16 validation isn't judgment quality — it's calibration: mean gap −0.77 tiers, −1.25 against Power Four, 5 of 15 defensive players caught. That gets fixed by more graded validation players and code, not by a different model.

## What I checked and discarded

**Player entity resolution** — dead. `PlayerId` is stable and already the join key. The Jordan Church / Louisville RG question is one cross-source name match against your recap list, and you already matched 30 of 30 transfers by hand. One player is not a pattern worth an API for.

**Role assignment (WR/SLOT, END/JACK, CB/STAR)** — this is the live blocker on 010, so I wanted it to fit. It doesn't. The inputs are alignment codes (OWR/SWR, ILB/OLB, OCB/SCB), which are already deterministic in both scripts, plus percentile numbers, which is Jev's documented weak spot. Nothing text-shaped to decide on.

# STATUS

Read this first. Update it before ending every session.

## Current state
- 2026-09-19: project created. Holds the global TypeSafe key installer and a smoke test.
- TypeSafe skill installed in Claude Code as plugin `typesafe@typesafe-ai` v0.5.7 (user scope).
- Key storage decided: macOS Keychain, service `typesafe-api-key`, exported by `~/.zshenv`.
  Chosen over a plaintext `.env` because `machine.macos.md` says secrets live in the Keychain,
  and because the `.zshenv` line contains no secret and is safe to commit.
- 2026-09-19: the plugin install and the API key are on the **Windows** box only. The Mac has
  the repo, the venv and the SDK, but neither the plugin nor the key. The `typesafe@typesafe-ai`
  line above describes Windows, not the Mac.
- 2026-09-19: cloned onto the Mac by dev-sync. Fixed the mode on `setup_global_key.sh`,
  which was committed 644, so `./setup_global_key.sh` failed with "permission denied".
- 2026-09-19: `.venv` built with `uv`, `typesafe-sdk==0.7.0` installed. `.venv/` is gitignored,
  so every machine builds its own.
- 2026-09-19: smoke test run on the Mac. It stops at the key guard and exits 1, which is
  correct behaviour. The test never reached the API from the Mac, so the Mac side of the
  call is still unproven there.
  What was checked separately against SDK 0.7.0: `TypeSafeClient.system_one(state=, questions=)`,
  `Noul(instructions=)` and `response.nouls[...].noul` all exist and match. Note that `nouls`
  is a property, not a model field, so it does not show up in `model_fields`.
- 2026-09-19: **the network call and authentication are now proven, on Windows.** This closes
  the two items left open above. Key added to `~/.claude/typesafe.env` and confirmed end to end
  against the real API. The first attempt failed 401 because the `apikey_` prefix had been

########## jev_client.py ##########
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal bounded client for the TypeSafe System One endpoint. Stdlib only.

Lifted from the skill router's `ask()`, which is the only HTTP path in this repo that
has been reviewed. The important property is the same here even though a batch job is
not latency-critical: **the timeout is real wall-clock time, not a socket timeout.**

`urlopen(timeout=)` bounds each individual blocking operation, so DNS, connect, TLS
and every body read each get the full value; a server trickling bytes never trips it.
The request therefore runs on a daemon thread and is abandoned if it overruns. In a
batch of 1,400 that is the difference between one slow record and a job that never
finishes.

NOTE: `skill_router/router.py` on branch `worktree-jev-skill-router` still carries its
own copy of this logic. When that branch merges, point it at this module so there is
one HTTP path rather than two that can drift.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import threading
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT", "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone")
MODEL = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_MODEL", "jev-latest")
MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024


class JevError(RuntimeError):
    """Anything that stopped us getting a usable answer."""


def api_key() -> str:
    """Env var first, then ~/.claude/typesafe.env.

    The key must keep its `apikey_` prefix. A 401 means the key value is wrong; a 422
    means the request body is. That split is the fastest way to tell which end is at
    fault, and it has cost this project time before.
    """
    key = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY")
    if key and key.strip():
        return key.strip()
    env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~")) / ".claude" / "typesafe.env"
    try:
        for line in env_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            name, _, value = line.strip().partition("=")
            if name.strip() == "TYPESAFE_API_KEY" and value.strip():
                return value.strip().strip("\"'")
    except OSError:
        pass
    raise JevError(
        "no TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment or ~/.claude/typesafe.env"
    )


def system_one(state, questions: dict, key: str, timeout: float = 20.0) -> dict:
    """POST one request and return its `answers` map. Raises JevError on anything else.

    No retries here on purpose: the caller owns retry policy, because what is safe to
    retry in a resumable batch job is not what is safe in a hook.
    """
    body = json.dumps(
        {"state": state, "model": MODEL, "questions": questions}
    ).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        ENDPOINT,
        data=body,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    outcome: dict = {}

    def perform() -> None:
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=timeout) as response:
                raw = response.read(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)
            outcome["data"] = json.loads(raw.decode("utf-8"))
        except BaseException as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - handed back to the caller
            outcome["error"] = error

    worker = threading.Thread(target=perform, daemon=True)
    worker.start()
    worker.join(timeout)
    if worker.is_alive():
        raise JevError(f"wall-clock timeout after {timeout}s")
    if "error" in outcome:
        raise JevError(f"{type(outcome['error']).__name__}: {outcome['error']}")

    payload = outcome.get("data")
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        raise JevError("response is not an object")
    answers = payload.get("answers")
    if not isinstance(answers, dict) or not answers:
        raise JevError("response carried no answers")
    return answers

# zotero_classify

Gives every research record in the Zotero library a topic, using TypeSafe's Jev. When
it is not confident enough to name one, it reports the broader domain instead, so
every record still gets a true label. Implements the `classification_using_confidence`
cookbook against a taxonomy drafted for this library.

Tier A: published literature and metadata only. No athlete data leaves the machine.

```bash
python taxonomy.py                 # print and sanity-check the taxonomy
python library.py                  # what the bridge index holds (read-only)
python validate.py --collect       # 41 hand-labelled records, ~41 calls
python validate.py                 # sweep the cutoff over saved answers, no calls
python classify.py --limit 20 --out runs/sample.jsonl   # try it small (new file)
python classify.py --out runs/full.jsonl                # all 1,418, ~86s, ~$0.07
python classify.py --out runs/full.jsonl --report       # re-read a run, no calls
python export.py                   # out/zotero_topics.csv + out/LIBRARY_MAP.md
```

Runs append to JSONL and skip records already done, so an interrupted run resumes and
a crash never costs the calls already paid for.

Needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the environment or in `~/.claude/typesafe.env`, keeping
its `apikey_` prefix. Needs the zotero-research bridge's `library.db`; override its
location with `ZOTERO_BRIDGE_DB`.

Design, measurements, the cutoff argument and the taxonomy mistake the first run
exposed: `../docs/ZOTERO_CLASSIFICATION.md`.

import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT", "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone")
MODEL = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_MODEL", "jev-latest")
MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024


class JevError(RuntimeError):
    """Anything that stopped us getting a usable answer."""


def api_key() -> str:
    """Env var first, then ~/.claude/typesafe.env.

    The key must keep its `apikey_` prefix. A 401 means the key value is wrong; a 422
    means the request body is. That split is the fastest way to tell which end is at
    fault, and it has cost this project time before.
    """
    key = os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY")
    if key and key.strip():
        return key.strip()
    env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~")) / ".claude" / "typesafe.env"
    try:
        for line in env_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            name, _, value = line.strip().partition("=")
            if name.strip() == "TYPESAFE_API_KEY" and value.strip():
                return value.strip().strip("\"'")
    except OSError:
        pass
    raise JevError(
        "no TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment or ~/.claude/typesafe.env"
    )


def system_one(state, questions: dict, key: str, timeout: float = 20.0) -> dict:
    """POST one request and return its `answers` map. Raises JevError on anything else.

    No retries here on purpose: the caller owns retry policy, because what is safe to
    retry in a resumable batch job is not what is safe in a hook.
    """
    body = json.dumps(
        {"state": state, "model": MODEL, "questions": questions}
    ).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        ENDPOINT,
        data=body,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    outcome: dict = {}

    def perform() -> None:
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=timeout) as response:
                raw = response.read(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)
            outcome["data"] = json.loads(raw.decode("utf-8"))
        except BaseException as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - handed back to the caller
            outcome["error"] = error

    worker = threading.Thread(target=perform, daemon=True)
    worker.start()
    worker.join(timeout)
    if worker.is_alive():
        raise JevError(f"wall-clock timeout after {timeout}s")
    if "error" in outcome:
        raise JevError(f"{type(outcome['error']).__name__}: {outcome['error']}")

    payload = outcome.get("data")
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        raise JevError("response is not an object")
    answers = payload.get("answers")
    if not isinstance(answers, dict) or not answers:
        raise JevError("response carried no answers")
    return answers

# zotero_classify

Gives every research record in the Zotero library a topic, using TypeSafe's Jev. When
it is not confident enough to name one, it reports the broader domain instead, so
every record still gets a true label. Implements the `classification_using_confidence`
cookbook against a taxonomy drafted for this library.

Tier A: published literature and metadata only. No athlete data leaves the machine.

```bash
python taxonomy.py                 # print and sanity-check the taxonomy
python library.py                  # what the bridge index holds (read-only)
python validate.py --collect       # 41 hand-labelled records, ~41 calls
python validate.py                 # sweep the cutoff over saved answers, no calls
python classify.py --limit 20 --out runs/sample.jsonl   # try it small (new file)
python classify.py --out runs/full.jsonl                # all 1,418, ~86s, ~$0.07
python classify.py --out runs/full.jsonl --report       # re-read a run, no calls
python export.py                   # out/zotero_topics.csv + out/LIBRARY_MAP.md
```

Runs append to JSONL and skip records already done, so an interrupted run resumes and
a crash never costs the calls already paid for.

Needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the environment or in `~/.claude/typesafe.env`, keeping
its `apikey_` prefix. Needs the zotero-research bridge's `library.db`; override its
location with `ZOTERO_BRIDGE_DB`.

Design, measurements, the cutoff argument and the taxonomy mistake the first run
exposed: `../docs/ZOTERO_CLASSIFICATION.md`.

content.content: # SDE cascade > Uses a 2-stage structured-data-extraction cascade (mini → verify → reasoning) to get most of the quality of a big reasoning model at a fraction of the cost. * Overview * big reasoning models extract structured data well, but are slow and expensive * small models are cheap, but make mistakes * a *cascade* gets most of the quality at a fraction of the cost * the models we use, and their price (\$ per 1M tokens, input / output; standard rates checked September 15, 2026): * rung 0 (mini): [`gpt-5.4-mini`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4-mini) at \$0.75 / \$4.50 * rung 1 (reasoning): [`gpt-5.5`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5) at \$5.00 / \$30.00 (roughly 7x the mini) * verifier: TypeSafe `jev-1.12` at \$0.042 / \$0.00 (output tokens are free; [published Jev pricing](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev)) * Algorithm 1. **Extract** with a cheap/small model. 2. **Verify** with **TypeSafe** primitives: a per-field yes/no ("Noul question") question * (e.g. "is this value absent from the source?", "was it lifted from unrelated text?"), each returning P(something is wrong). 3. **Escalate** to an expensive reasoning model if a verifier signal fires; otherwise keep the cheap answer. * This Cookbook * walks one real example end-to-end, then shows the tradeoff across 100 prompts * note: the two extraction rungs use text-mode OpenAI * we do *not* use structured outputs, tool calls, or json mode, because: * a *schema following* mistake is not the mistake we expect an LLM to make (it's easy to make synthetic data for this) * if an LLM does fail to follow the schema, it's almost always very confused, so constrained decoding doesn't fix the underlying issue * we encourage you to try them though! ## Setup * install the dependencies (the TypeSafe verifier client is served from TypeSafe's package index): ```bash theme={null} pip install openai datasets jsonschema ipython "typesafe-sdk>=0.5.7" cooksafe --extra-index-url https://pypi.typesafe.ai/ ``` * then set `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in your environment ```python theme={null} import json import os from pathlib import Path import jsonschema from cooksafe import JsonCache, make_playground_link from datasets import load_dataset from IPython.display import Markdown, display from openai import OpenAI from typesafe_sdk import Noul, NoulCriteria, TypeSafeClient MINI = "gpt-5.4-mini" # rung 0: cheap + fast REASONING = "gpt-5.5" # rung 1: strong, run with reasoning_effort="high" TS_MODEL = "jev-1.12" # the TypeSafe verifier model FIRE_T = 0.7 # escalate if any per-field P(wrong) exceeds this; also the "<== FIRES" display marker oai = OpenAI() ts = TypeSafeClient(api_key=os.environ["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"], timeout=30.0) ``` ## Step 1: the data We choose a huggingface dataset called scrapegraphai ```python theme={null} SCRAPEGRAPHAI_REVISION = "4bb9fba1dff9181c5acdb60a5a26fea62fa54fe9" row = load_dataset( "scrapegraphai/scrapegraphai-100k", revision=SCRAPEGRAPHAI_REVISION, split="train", )[516] schema = json.loads(row["schema"]) prompt = row["prompt"] content = row["content"] print( f""" PROMPT =========== {prompt} SCHEMA =========== {json.dumps(schema, indent=2)} CONTENT =========== {content} """.strip() ) ``` ```text expandable theme={null} PROMPT =========== Find registration open date fall semester for New York University in New York, NY for the 2024-2025 school year. ## Step 2: extract with the mini model (text mode) * note: `gpt-5.4-mini` is very stochastic on this input -- even at `temperature=0` it invents a different `description` on nearly every run. For a reproducible walkthrough we **hard-code** the one canonical fabrication the rest of this notebook explains (and that the verifier flags at P(wrong) > 0.8). A real pipeline would just take `extract(MINI, prompt, schema, content, temperature=0)` directly. ```python expandable theme={null} EXTRACT_SYSTEM = ( "You extract structured data from documents. " "Follow any value format specified by the schema or its field descriptions." ) # LLM and TypeSafe calls are cached to ``json_cache.json``, which ships with the cookbook, so # re-rendering reproduces the published results with no API spend; delete the file to re-run live. json_cache = JsonCache(Path("json_cache.json")) @json_cache def extract( model: str, prompt: str, schema: dict, content: str, *, reasoning_effort: str | None = None, temperature: float | None = None, ) -> dict: user = ( f"{prompt}\n\nReturn ONLY a JSON object matching this JSON Schema:\n" f"{json.dumps(schema, indent=2)}\n\nDocument:\n{content}" ) kwargs = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": EXTRACT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": user}, ], } if reasoning_effort: kwargs["reasoning_effort"] = reasoning_effort if temperature is not None: kwargs["temperature"] = temperature text = oai.chat.completions.create(**kwargs).choices[0].message.content # The prompt asks for ONLY a JSON object, so parse the reply as-is -- no regex fishing a # substring out of a malformed reply. It may parrot the schema's own example, "Registration opens for the fall semester", or narrate "...was not found in the document" * a JSON-Schema check can't see this. A cheap model produces confident, schema-satisfying fabrications of this kind, and catching them is the job of a semantic verifier ## Step 3: verify with TypeSafe * the verifier is **TypeSafe**; for each field we build a `Noul` question: * a narrow yes/no, framed so that `true` = something is wrong (escalate) * TypeSafe returns a calibrated `noul` = `P(true)` per question, in one system\_one call * the question set: * one holistic **`__overall__::judge`** head ("should this record be escalated?"). We compute and display it to contrast a whole-record judgment with the per-field heads, but the gate in Step 4 does **not** use it -- escalation is driven by the per-field battery. * a per-field battery * non-empty fields get the full set of heads * empty fields (null / "" / \[]) get only the `absence_wrong` head * (the full pipeline also has a `spurious` head for whole containers and an overall `difficulty` score; not shown here, to keep this walkthrough to the two gating heads) * **The TypeSafe Way: Decomposition** * Notice how everything is *programmatically decomposed*, this is TypeSafe way. * Decomposition maximizes the intelligence of every prompt, and makes the algorithm tunable and interpretable. * ```python expandable theme={null} # metric -> (question, NoulCriteria) MAIN_QUESTIONS = { "name_desc_mismatch": ( "Does the `extracted_field` fail to match the field at `path` or the `description` in the " "`field_spec`? OVERALL_JUDGE = ( "Is this extracted record an incorrect extraction -- some value unsupported by the source or " "not conforming to the schema, required information missing or wrong, or some field hallucinated -- " "so it should be escalated to a smarter model?" ) OVERALL_JUDGE_CRITERIA = NoulCriteria( true="the record is an incorrect extraction", false="the record is a correct extraction", ) def is_empty(v) -> bool: return v is None or (isinstance(v, (str, list, dict)) and len(v) == 0) def field_spec(name: str) -> dict: """Minimal spec pulled from the schema (unwrapping anyOf/null for optional fields).""" p = schema["properties"][name] branches = p.get("anyOf") or [] typ = p.get("type") or next( (b["type"] for b in branches if b.get("type") != "null"), "unknown" ) return { "path": holistic ``__overall__::judge`` head plus a per-field battery, keyed ``field::metric`` (mirrors build_verify_prompts).""" questions: dict[str, Noul] = { "__overall__::judge": Noul( criteria=criteria, ) return questions @json_cache def verify(record: dict) -> dict[str, float | str]: """Run the whole Noul battery over a record in one TypeSafe call; return ``{field::metric: P(true)}``.""" state = { "system_message": EXTRACT_SYSTEM, "instruction": "Extract the structured record from this document", "source_text": row["content"], "schema": schema, "extraction": record, } display( Markdown( f"🔗 [Open this verification in the TypeSafe playground]({playground_link})" ) ) print(f"{'qid':<40}{'P(wrong)':>9}") print("-" * 50) for fld, p in sorted(checks.items(), key=lambda c: -c[-1]): flag = " <== FIRES" if p > FIRE_T else "" print(f"{fld:<40}{p:>9.2f}{flag}") ``` ``` qid P(wrong) -------------------------------------------------- description::hallucinated 0.95 <== FIRES description::off_target 0.85 <== FIRES description::unreasonable 0.58 __overall__::judge 0.56 description::incomplete 0.16 registration_open_date::absence_wrong 0.14 description::format_violation 0.10 description::name_desc_mismatch 0.08 description::type_mismatch 0.02 ``` * TypeSafe concentrates the signal on the fields that are actually wrong. * Our results are calibrated: high on the field that is wrong, low on the field that is correct, medium on a field that looks off without being clearly wrong * This is what a typesafe verifier buys you over a blunt "is this whole thing good?" judge ## Step 4: the escalation gate * now we gate on **`any_flag`**: escalate if *any* field flag exceeds `FIRE_T` (0.7, set above and shared with the `<== FIRES` marker in Step 3) * this is a `max`-style gate (escalate if *any* field fires), not a mean, so one confident red flag is enough instead of being averaged into silence ```python theme={null} # any_flag is a per-field gate: the holistic __overall__ head is shown above but not part of it fired = { qid: p for qid, p in checks.items() if not qid.startswith("__overall__") and p > FIRE_T } escalate = bool(fired) print( f"any_flag gate (threshold {FIRE_T}): {'ESCALATE' if escalate else 'ACCEPT cheap result'}" ) for qid, p in sorted(fired.items(), key=lambda c: -c[1]): print(f" fired: {qid} (P={p:.2f})") ``` ``` any_flag gate (threshold 0.7): ESCALATE fired: description::hallucinated (P=0.95) fired: description::off_target (P=0.85) ``` ## Step 5: escalate to the reasoning model Since a signal fired, we pay for the strong model (`gpt-5.5`, `reasoning_effort="high"`) ```python theme={null} final_record = ( extract(REASONING, prompt, schema, content, reasoning_effort="high") if escalate else mini_record ) print("mini :", json.dumps(mini_record)) print("reasoning :", json.dumps(final_record)) print("\nfield-level diff (mini -> final):") for name in mini_record: if mini_record[name] != final_record.get(name): print(f" {name}: {mini_record[name]!r} -> {final_record.get(name)!r}") ``` ``` mini : {"registration_open_date": "", "description": "Registration opens for the fall semester"} reasoning : {"description": "", "registration_open_date": ""} field-level diff (mini -> final): description: 'Registration opens for the fall semester' -> '' ``` * **The improvement** * The reasoning model drops the fabricated `description`, returning `""` * It recognized the page never describes a registration date, and declined to invent one * The cascade turned a confident, schema-valid fabrication into an honest empty field * And it only spent reasoning-model dollars on this one item *because the verifier told it to* ## Step 6: what this looks like on 100 prompts * **These are internal TypeSafe results**, produced with the general method above: * the same `extract → verify → escalate` loop, `gpt-5.4-mini → gpt-5.5-reasoning`, `any_flag` gate over the per-field heads, run over 100 scrapegraphai prompts * each item's cheap-rung extraction is scored by TypeSafe; the gate threshold ("cut") is swept 0→1, and every resulting config is plotted in (cost, quality) space * the chart is a historical snapshot; its costs have not been recalculated at the current Jev rate listed above * how to read it: * **black diamonds** = the four models run on their own (cost climbs with capability; the strongest, `gpt-5.5-reasoning`, sits top-right at ≈0.81 quality for ≈\$0.10/extraction) * **blue points** = the cascade at many gate thresholds; the dashed line is the **pareto frontier** * the cascade frontier sits **up-and-left of every single model**: sweeping the gate buys you most of the top model's quality at a fraction of its cost * the cheap rung handles the easy items for near-free, and only the flagged items pay for the reasoning model ## Appendix A: what makes a good verifier signal * the cascade is only as good as its verifier; what separates a useful signal from a useless one: * **Narrow and grounded.** * one checkable yes/no about one field against the source (e.g. "is this value absent from the source?"), not a vague "is this extraction good?" * vague questions give mushy, uncalibrated scores * **Bad = TRUE, with explicit criteria.** * frame each question so the *escalate* case is the `true` case, and state what `true`/`false` mean * **Per-field, then aggregate with `max`.** * a per-field flag localizes the error and stays sparse and strong * `max` ("any flag fires") ensures one confident red flag escalates, instead of being averaged into silence * **Independent and cheap.** * a dedicated verifier (here, TypeSafe) judging the output catches the extractor's own blind spots * it has to be cheap, or there are no savings left to capture * **Separating / calibrated.** * a good signal is high on real errors and low on correct ones, so a single threshold cleanly splits accept vs escalate * that separation is what pushes the ## Step 2: extract with the mini model (text mode) * note: `gpt-5.4-mini` is very stochastic on this input -- even at `temperature=0` it invents a different `description` on nearly every run. For a reproducible walkthrough we **hard-code** the one canonical fabrication the rest of this notebook explains (and that the verifier flags at P(wrong) > 0.8). A real pipeline would just take `extract(MINI, prompt, schema, content, temperature=0)` directly. ```python expandable theme={null} EXTRACT_SYSTEM = ( "You extract structured data from documents. Return only values supported by the text. " "Follow any value format specified by the schema or its field descriptions." ) # LLM and TypeSafe calls are cached to ``json_cache.json``, which ships with the cookbook, so # re-rendering reproduces the published results with no API spend; delete the file to re-run live. json_cache = JsonCache(Path("json_cache.json")) @json_cache def extract( model: str, prompt: str, schema: dict, content: str, *, reasoning_effort: str | None = None, temperature: float | None = None, ) -> dict: user = ( f"{prompt}\n\nReturn ONLY a JSON object matching this JSON Schema:\n" f"{json.dumps(schema, indent=2)}\n\nDocument:\n{content}" ) kwargs = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": EXTRACT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": user}, ], } if reasoning_effort: kwargs["reasoning_effort"] = reasoning_effort if temperature is not None: kwargs["temperature"] = temperature text = oai.chat.completions.create(**kwargs).choices[0].message.content # The prompt asks for ONLY a JSON object, so parse the reply as-is -- no regex fishing a # substring out of a malformed reply. If ``json.loads`` fails, treat it as an empty extraction # (the record-level analog of NaN): every field reads as absent, which the verifier flags and the # gate escalates -- the safe direction. Schema-following errors are rare here (see the overview). try: return json.loads(text) except (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError): return {} # Hard-coded canonical fabrication (see note above); a real pipeline would use extract(MINI, prompt, schema, content, temperature=0). mini_record = { "registration_open_date": "", "description": "Registration opens for the fall semester", } print("mini extraction:\n", json.dumps(mini_record, indent=2)) # The record is a perfect fit for the JSON Schema -- and still wrong. Schema validation is necessary # but not sufficient: it catches structural errors, never semantic ones. That gap is the whole point. print("\nschema-valid:", jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(schema).is_valid(mini_record)) ``` ``` mini extraction: { "registration_open_date": "", "description": "Registration opens for the fall semester" } schema-valid: True ``` * The record is **schema-valid** (the line above prints `True`), yet it's wrong: * `registration_open_date` is left blank, which matches the page: it states no date * but `description` is fabricated: the page never describes a registration date, so mini invents a plausible one. It may parrot the schema's own example, "Registration opens for the fall semester", or narrate "...was not found in the document" * a JSON-Schema check can't see this. A cheap model produces confident, schema-satisfying fabrications of this kind, and catching them is the job of a semantic verifier ## Step 3: verify with TypeSafe * the verifier is **TypeSafe**; for each field we build a `Noul` question: * a narrow yes/no, framed so that `true` = something is wrong (escalate) * TypeSafe returns a calibrated `noul` = `P(true)` per question, in one system\_one call * the question set: * one holistic **`__overall__::judge`** head ("should this record be escalated?"). We compute and display it to contrast a whole-record judgment with the per-field heads, but the gate in Step 4 does **not** use it -- escalation is driven by the per-field battery. * a per-field battery * non-empty fields get the full set of heads * empty fields (null / "" / \[]) get only the `absence_wrong` head * (the full pipeline also has a `spurious` head for whole containers and an overall `difficulty` score; not shown here, to keep this walkthrough to the two gating heads) * **The TypeSafe Way: Decomposition** * Notice how everything is *programmatically decomposed*, this is TypeSafe way. * Decomposition maximizes the intelligence of every prompt, and makes the algorithm tunable and interpretable. * ```python expandable theme={null} # metric -> (question, NoulCriteria) MAIN_QUESTIONS = { "name_desc_mismatch": ( "Does the `extracted_field` fail to match the field at `path` or the `description` in the " "`field_spec`? If the `description` is empty, judge against the `path` alone.", NoulCriteria( true="the `extracted_field` does not match the field name or its `description`", false="the `extracted_field` matches the field name and `description`", ), ), "type_mismatch": ( "Does the `extracted_field` violate the `type` declared in the `field_spec`?", NoulCriteria( true="the `extracted_field` violates the declared `type`", false="the `extracted_field` conforms to the declared `type`", ), ), "unreasonable": ( "Is the `extracted_field` one that a reasonable person would not have extracted for this " "`field_spec`?", NoulCriteria( true="a reasonable person would not have extracted this value", false="the extraction is reasonable", ), ), "hallucinated": ( "Is the `extracted_field` unsupported by, or absent from, the source text?", NoulCriteria( true="the `extracted_field` is a hallucination -- not supported by, or absent " "from, the source text", false="the `extracted_field` is supported by the source text", ), ), "off_target": ( "Does the source text fail to genuinely report the thing the `field_spec` describes, so the " "value was pulled from incidental text?", NoulCriteria( true="the source does not genuinely provide this field -- the value was pulled " "from incidental text", false="the source genuinely reports this field", ), ), "incomplete": ( "Does the `extracted_field` fail to capture a value the source supports (note whether the " "`field_spec` is `required`)?", NoulCriteria( true="the field is wrongly empty, null, or missing a value the source supports", false="the field captures the value the source supports", ), ), "format_violation": ( "Does the `extracted_field` violate the format or constraints implied by the `description`, " "the schema `type`, and the extraction instructions (e.g. date format, units, enum membership)?", NoulCriteria( true="the `extracted_field` violates the implied format or constraints", false="the `extracted_field` satisfies the format and constraints", ), ), } ABSENCE_QUESTION = ( "The `extracted_field` is empty, null, or an empty collection. Does the source text contain the " "information the `field_spec` describes, making the empty result wrong?" ) ABSENCE_CRITERIA = NoulCriteria( true="a value was wrongly omitted", false="returning nothing is correct" ) # The pipeline also asks one holistic, whole-record head: "should this be escalated?" OVERALL_JUDGE = ( "Is this extracted record an incorrect extraction -- some value unsupported by the source or " "not conforming to the schema, required information missing or wrong, or some field hallucinated -- " "so it should be escalated to a smarter model?" ) OVERALL_JUDGE_CRITERIA = NoulCriteria( true="the record is an incorrect extraction", false="the record is a correct extraction", ) def is_empty(v) -> bool: return v is None or (isinstance(v, (str, list, dict)) and len(v) == 0) def field_spec(name: str) -> dict: """Minimal spec pulled from the schema (unwrapping anyOf/null for optional fields).""" p = schema["properties"][name] branches = p.get("anyOf") or [] typ = p.get("type") or next( (b["type"] for b in branches if b.get("type") != "null"), "unknown" ) return { "path": name, "type": typ, "description": p.get("description", ""), "required": name in schema.get("required", []), } def build_questions(record: dict) -> dict[str, Noul]: """The verify question set: one holistic ``__overall__::judge`` head plus a per-field battery, keyed ``field::metric`` (mirrors build_verify_prompts).""" questions: dict[str, Noul] = { "__overall__::judge": Noul( instructions=OVERALL_JUDGE, criteria=OVERALL_JUDGE_CRITERIA ), } for name, value in record.items(): spec = field_spec(name) if is_empty(value): questions[f"{name}::absence_wrong"] = Noul( instructions={ "field_spec": spec, "extracted_field": value, "main_question": ABSENCE_QUESTION, }, criteria=ABSENCE_CRITERIA, ) continue for metric, (question, criteria) in MAIN_QUESTIONS.items(): if metric == "type_mismatch" and spec["type"] == "unknown": continue questions[f"{name}::{metric}"] = Noul( instructions={ "field_spec": spec, "extracted_field": value, "main_question": question, }, criteria=criteria, ) return questions @json_cache def verify(record: dict) -> dict[str, float | str]: """Run the whole Noul battery over a record in one TypeSafe call; return ``{field::metric: P(true)}``.""" state = { "system_message": EXTRACT_SYSTEM, "instruction": "Extract the structured record from this document", "source_text": row["content"], "schema": schema, "extraction": record, } questions = build_questions(record) answers = ts.system_one(state=state, questions=questions, model=TS_MODEL).answers return {qid: ans.noul for qid, ans in answers.items()} | { "playground_link": make_playground_link(state, questions) } ``` ### Run the whole battery over the mini extraction ```python theme={null} checks = verify(mini_record) playground_link = checks.pop("playground_link") display( Markdown( f"🔗 [Open this verification in the TypeSafe playground]({playground_link})" ) ) print(f"{'qid':<40}{'P(wrong)':>9}") print("-" * 50) for fld, p in sorted(checks.items(), key=lambda c: -c[-1]): flag = " <== FIRES" if p > FIRE_T else "" print(f"{fld:<40}{p:>9.2f}{flag}") ``` ``` qid P(wrong) -------------------------------------------------- description::hallucinated 0.95 <== FIRES description::off_target 0.85 <== FIRES description::unreasonable 0.58 __overall__::judge 0.56 description::incomplete 0.16 registration_open_date::absence_wrong 0.14 description::format_violation 0.10 description::name_desc_mismatch 0.08 description::type_mismatch 0.02 ``` * TypeSafe concentrates the signal on the fields that are actually wrong. * Our results are calibrated: high on the field that is wrong, low on the field that is correct, medium on a field that looks off without being clearly wrong * This is what a typesafe verifier buys you over a blunt "is this whole thing good?" judge ## Step 4: the escalation gate * now we gate on **`any_flag`**: escalate if *any* field flag exceeds `FIRE_T` (0.7, set above and shared with the `<== FIRES` marker in Step 3) * this is a `max`-style gate (escalate if *any* field fires), not a mean, so one confident red flag is enough instead of being averaged into silence ```python theme={null} # any_flag is a per-field gate: the holistic __overall__ head is shown above but not part of it fired = { qid: p for qid, p in checks.items() if not qid.startswith("__overall__") and p > FIRE_T } escalate = bool(fired) print( f"any_flag gate (threshold {FIRE_T}): {'ESCALATE' if escalate else 'ACCEPT cheap result'}" ) for qid, p in sorted(fired.items(), key=lambda c: -c[1]): print(f" fired: {qid} (P={p:.2f})") ``` ``` any_flag gate (threshold 0.7): ESCALATE fired: description::hallucinated (P=0.95) fired: description::off_target (P=0.85) ``` ## Step 5: escalate to the reasoning model Since a signal fired, we pay for the strong model (`gpt-5.5`, `reasoning_effort="high"`) ```python theme={null} final_record = ( extract(REASONING, prompt, schema, content, reasoning_effort="high") if escalate else mini_record ) print("mini :", json.dumps(mini_record)) print("reasoning :", json.dumps(final_record)) print("\nfield-level diff (mini -> final):") for name in mini_record: if mini_record[name] != final_record.get(name): print(f" {name}: {mini_record[name]!r} -> {final_record.get(name)!r}") ``` ``` mini : {"registration_open_date": "", "description": "Registration opens for the fall semester"} reasoning : {"description": "", "registration_open_date": ""} field-level diff (mini -> final): description: 'Registration opens for the fall semester' -> '' ``` * **The improvement** * The reasoning model drops the fabricated `description`, returning `""` * It recognized the page never describes a registration date, and declined to invent one * The cascade turned a confident, schema-valid fabrication into an honest empty field * And it only spent reasoning-model dollars on this one item *because the verifier told it to* ## Step 6: what this looks like on 100 prompts * **These are internal TypeSafe results**, produced with the general method above: * the same `extract → verify → escalate` loop, `gpt-5.4-mini → gpt-5.5-reasoning`, `any_flag` gate over the per-field heads, run over 100 scrapegraphai prompts * each item's cheap-rung extraction is scored by TypeSafe; the gate threshold ("cut") is swept 0→1, and every resulting config is plotted in (cost, quality) space * the chart is a historical snapshot; its costs have not been recalculated at the current Jev rate listed above * how to read it: * **black diamonds** = the four models run on their own (cost climbs with capability; the strongest, `gpt-5.5-reasoning`, sits top-right at ≈0.81 quality for ≈\$0.10/extraction) * **blue points** = the cascade at many gate thresholds; the dashed line is the **pareto frontier** * the cascade frontier sits **up-and-left of every single model**: sweeping the gate buys you most of the top model's quality at a fraction of its cost * the cheap rung handles the easy items for near-free, and only the flagged items pay for the reasoning model ## Appendix A: what makes a good verifier signal * the cascade is only as good as its verifier; what separates a useful signal from a useless one: * **Narrow and grounded.** * one checkable yes/no about one field against the source (e.g. "is this value absent from the source?"), not a vague "is this extraction good?" * vague questions give mushy, uncalibrated scores * **Bad = TRUE, with explicit criteria.** * frame each question so the *escalate* case is the `true` case, and state what `true`/`false` mean * **Per-field, then aggregate with `max`.** * a per-field flag localizes the error and stays sparse and strong * `max` ("any flag fires") ensures one confident red flag escalates, instead of being averaged into silence * **Independent and cheap.** * a dedicated verifier (here, TypeSafe) judging the output catches the extractor's own blind spots * it has to be cheap, or there are no savings left to capture * **Separating / calibrated.** * a good signal is high on real errors and low on correct ones, so a single threshold cleanly splits accept vs escalate * that separation is what pushes the pareto curve up-and-left

entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

# Deliverable verifier — Research in 5

Third item in the capability map's sequence, after the skill router and the Zotero
classification. Checks a Research in 5 deck against the paper it claims to report,
before it is sent.

Built 2026-09-19 from the `citation_check` cookbook, with the aggregation rule from
`sde_cascade`. Code in `verifier/`.

**Governance: tier A.** A published paper and a deck written about it. No athlete
data, no health records.

## Why this one

The capability map called it "the one I would not have predicted". The concrete
motivation is in memory: the TOS brief was stopped on 2026-09-18 with *"3 misquotes +
bad Poisson — DO NOT SEND"*, caught by hand. Research in 5 goes out every week, to
staff, with Eric's name on it. A misquoted mean in a slide table is both easy to
produce and hard to spot by rereading your own work.

## Result

Against review 001 (Saraee et al., jumper's knee alignment), hand-checked to v4 and
marked ready to send:

| | |
|---|---|
| claims extracted | **67** — 50 numeric, 17 prose |
| verified | 59 |
| routed to a person | 8 |
| **false alarms** | **0** |
| wall time | **1.4 s** |
| cost | a fraction of a cent (17 calls) |

And against the same deck with defects planted in it, one per failure class
(`python test_verify.py`):

| planted | expected | caught |
|---|---|---|
| table mean `83.89` → `84.89` | fabricated | ✅ 2 claims |
| table source `p. 6` → `p. 4` | wrong_page | ✅ 21 claims |
| "None of the 7" → "Five of the 7 reached significance" | contradicted | ✅ 1 claim |
| sample size `22` → `93` | fabricated | ✅ 1 claim |

**4 of 4 caught, 0 false alarms on the real deck.** Finding nothing wrong with a deck
that is already correct proves very little on its own — a verifier that always says
"clear" would score the same — so the planted defects are the actual evidence.

## The design decision that matters: what counts as a claim

`review.json` is a deck, not a list of citations, so the extraction *is* the design.
It happens in `claims.py`, deterministically, in code, and sorts every claim into one
of three kinds:

**Numbers** — every table cell, chart value and numeric headline figure. Checked by
**string match only; these never go to Jev.** The capability map is explicit that the
half which catches a misquoted number is the code match, and the jaggedness page is
explicit that Jev is unreliable at arithmetic and at comparing numeric
representations. Asking a model whether 83.89 appears in a table is using the wrong
tool for a job `float()` does perfectly.

**Cited prose** — anything naming a page, plus derived figures like `0 of 7` and `<1°`
which are computed *from* the paper rather than printed in it. One Choice against the
page the deck itself cites.

**Uncited prose** — everything else. The best page is chosen **in code by keyword
overlap before any call**, then one Choice against that page. Sending all 11 pages
would both blow the 32k state budget and invite the documented context-rot failure;
the docs' instruction is to filter in code and send only what the question needs.

### What is deliberately not checked

`meaning.roles[].line`, `meaning.summary` and `hook`. These are Eric's practitioner
inferences and framing — *"We can't train bone angles. We can coach landings."* They
are not claims about what the paper says, and asking supports/contradicts of them
produces confident `says_nothing`, i.e. a pile of false unsupported-claims. A tool
that cries wolf on the writer's own judgement is a tool that gets ignored. Whether an
inference is *reasonable* is a good question and a different prompt; it is not this
pass.

`did.question` was cut for the same reason, but only after it failed. It holds the
question the study asked — *"If only one knee hurts, is that leg lined up
differently?"* — and Jev returned **contradicts** on it, correctly, because the
paper's answer is no. The verifier reported a sound deck as contradicted. A question
asserts nothing, so supports/contradicts has nothing to grip. Only assertions are
checked this way.

## Verdicts, and why the deck's verdict is the worst one

```
fabricated    a figure that is nowhere in the paper
contradicted  the page says the opposite
wrong_page    the figure is real, but not on the page the deck cites
unsupported   the page does not address the claim
review        Jev answered below the confidence floor; a person decides
verified      checked and sound
```

The deck's verdict is the **maximum severity across all claims**, never a count or a
mean. That is the `sde_cascade` rule, and it is the point: one confident red flag has
to survive rather than being averaged into silence by fifty-nine green ones. `verify.py`
exits non-zero on anything above `review`, so it can gate a send.

`wrong_page` earns its own verdict rather than being folded into `verified`. The
numbers are real and the attribution is wrong, which is both an easy mistake to make
when a deck is revised and a specific embarrassment when a coach follows the citation.

## The bug that proves the point about false alarms

The first run reported `87.5` as **fabricated**. The paper prints `87.50`.

The original matcher worked on strings with a boundary check — right for stopping
`1.78` matching inside `41.783`, wrong for `87.5` against `87.50`, where the very next
character is a digit. No amount of string-variant generation fixes that class
properly. The comparison is now numeric: every figure on a page is parsed to a float
and compared as a number.

Equality stays **exact**. 87.5 and 87.50 are the same number and must match; 83.89 and
83.9 are a real discrepancy in a results table and must not. Rounding to a shared
precision would hide precisely the misquote this exists to catch.

## Honest limits

- **Eight of seventeen prose claims land in `review`** at the 0.80 confidence floor —
  nearly half. The cookbook says to start high and lower it as the model earns trust,
  and 0.80 is its starting value, but there is **no measurement here** that says 0.80
  is right for these decks. Tuning it properly needs a hand-labelled set of prose
  claims the way the Zotero cutoff got one. Until then, `review` means "a person
  reads it", and eight items is a few minutes' work on a weekly deliverable.

  **There is already evidence of what lowering it would cost.** The claim
  *"0 of 7 angles were different between the two knees"* came back `supports` at 0.36
  on one run and `contradicts` at 0.30 on the next, from identical input. That is the
  documented near-threshold label flip — the jaggedness page measures 2 of 8 questions
  changing their top label across 15 repeats — and `review` caught it both times,
  which is the uncertain band doing exactly its job. Drop the floor to 0.25 and that
  same correct claim reports the deck as CONTRADICTED on some runs and clear on
  others. Lower the threshold against labels, not against the wish for fewer items.
- **One deck, one paper.** Everything above is measured on review 001, and that is
  still the only deck this has been shown to work on. Review 002 and the TOS brief
  were both tried; neither could be checked against its sources, for the reasons in
  the next section.
- **Page-level text must exist** in the bridge index. A paper synced without
  `include_fulltext` has no pages and the verifier says so rather than guessing.
- **The uncited-prose page choice is keyword overlap**, which is crude. It reports the
  overlap it used in every verdict line so a wrong page is visible rather than silent.

## Files

| file | what it does |
|---|---|
| `verifier/claims.py` | pulls claims out of `review.json` and sorts them into three kinds |
| `verifier/source.py` | page-level paper text from the bridge index, read-only; numeric matching |
| `verifier/verify.py` | the check, the verdicts, the CLI |
| `verifier/test_verify.py` | the real deck plus four planted defects |

It imports `jev_client.py` from `zotero_classify/` rather than carrying a third copy
of the HTTP path. That client's own docstring asks for exactly this.

```bash
cd verifier
python claims.py <review.json>     # what would be checked, and how
python verify.py --review <review.json>
python verify.py --review <review.json> --json
python test_verify.py              # baseline + the four planted defects
```

## Pointed at the TOS brief: it did not catch the known errors

The TOS evidence brief was the designed test — memory records it stopped on 2026-09-18
with *"3 misquotes + bad Poisson — DO NOT SEND"*, so the errors are known in advance.
The doc said before running it that failing to flag them would be a finding about the
verifier. It failed to flag them, and here is the finding.

**First, two hard blockers, both verified rather than assumed:**

- **Research in 5 #002 cannot be checked.** Its `paper.zotero_key` is empty (sourced by
  DOI), and the Funakoshi paper is not in the Zotero library at all — searched by DOI,
  title and author, zero hits. Its `stats[].page` values are also *journal* pages
  (625), not PDF pages, which is a numbering mismatch the project's own gotchas warn
  about. The handoff separately records that **#002 is unaffected** by the TOS errors,
  so it was never the right target anyway.
- **The TOS brief's sources are not in Zotero either.** All 109 came from PubMed.
  Kamarajugadda, Takaba, Ulman and Talutis — the four behind the known errors — return
  zero hits. Without a source paper there is nothing to verify a claim *against*, so
  the deck verifier does not apply to this document at all.
  `verifier/tos_sources/` holds a one-paste import kit; Claude cannot import them,
  because the bridge key is read-only (`write: false`) and Zotero was not running.

**So a second check was built** (`verify_brief.py`) that asks a question this document
uniquely allows: the brief presents its evidence and its conclusion in the same
section, so *does the evidence shown carry the claim made?* That directly targets what
Codex said the problem was — *"the risk comes from the final inferential step"*.

It ran over 145 bolded claims in 8.8 s. It did not work well enough to use:

| | |
|---|---|
| supported | 12 |
| **review** | **113 (78%)** |
| unsupported | 4 |
| overstated | 16 |

And on the three claims that are known to be wrong:

| known misquote | Jev's top choice | confidence | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "roughly half of true pitch volume is invisible" | `overstates` | 0.27 | review |
| "the cocked position roughly **doubles** scalene stiffness" | `overstates` | 0.50 | review |
| "LE screening predicted 49.9% of shoulder distraction variance" | `says_nothing` | 0.44 | review |

**The direction is right on two of three and the confidence is nowhere near usable.**
All three land in `review`, where they are indistinguishable from 113 others.

### Why, and it is structural rather than a tuning problem

Look at what those two errors actually are. Takaba measured **14.4 vs 9.4 kPa**; the
brief calls that *"roughly doubles"*. It is 53%. Kamarajugadda measured **51.2% of
outings exceeding a recommendation**; the brief calls that *"roughly half of true pitch
volume"*. Both numbers are real, correctly transcribed, and sitting in the same
section as the claim.

That puts this class of error **between both mechanisms**:

- the **string match** passes, because every figure is present and correct;
- the **model** is being asked whether 14.4 against 9.4 is "roughly double", which is
  arithmetic — the one thing the jaggedness page says Jev is unreliable at, and the
  reason numbers were routed away from it in the first place.

A correct number, correctly quoted, wrongly characterised in words is the gap. Lowering
`AUTO_ACCEPT` does not close it: at a floor low enough to surface `overstates` at 0.27,
the 113 review items become 113 assertions and the tool is worse than nothing.

**What would close it** is a third mechanism, in code: extract (figure, characterising
word) pairs — "doubles", "roughly half", "an order of magnitude", "most" — and check
the arithmetic. 14.4/9.4 = 1.53, which is not "doubles"; that is a two-line comparison
once the pair is extracted, and it needs no model. That is the honest next build, and
it is a better use of effort than tuning a threshold.

### Smaller thing fixed on the way

Three of the four question-shaped lines in the brief came back flagged — the "Open
questions worth answering locally" section is entirely questions. Exactly the category
error already fixed in the deck verifier for `did.question`, not ported across.
Questions are now skipped here too, which is why the claim count is 145 rather than 149.

## Next

- **Build the figure-versus-characterisation check.** The TOS run above says this is
  where the real gap is: a correct number described in words the arithmetic does not
  support. It is a code check, not a model one, and it needs no new API surface.
- **Import the four TOS source papers** (`verifier/tos_sources/README.md`) so the brief
  can be checked against its sources rather than only against itself. Needs Eric: the
  bridge key is read-only.
- **Tune `AUTO_ACCEPT` against hand labels**, rather than leaving it at the cookbook's
  starting value.
- **Wire it into the Research in 5 workflow** so a deck cannot be published without
  passing. It is a CLI that exits non-zero for exactly this reason, but nothing calls
  it yet — `build.js` or the `/research-in-5` skill is the hook point.
- Then the status report, which needs reading first: if its fields name athletes or
  injuries, that content is tier B or C and cannot go to a cloud API as it stands.

  DOI), and the Funakoshi paper is not in the Zotero library at all — searched by DOI,
  title and author, zero hits. Its `stats[].page` values are also *journal* pages
  (625), not PDF pages, which is a numbering mismatch the project's own gotchas warn
  about. The handoff separately records that **#002 is unaffected** by the TOS errors,
  so it was never the right target anyway.
- **The TOS brief's sources are not in Zotero either.** All 109 came from PubMed.
  Kamarajugadda, Takaba, Ulman and Talutis — the four behind the known errors — return
  zero hits. Without a source paper there is nothing to verify a claim *against*, so
  the deck verifier does not apply to this document at all.
  `verifier/tos_sources/` holds a one-paste import kit; Claude cannot import them,
  because the bridge key is read-only (`write: false`) and Zotero was not running.

**So a second check was built** (`verify_brief.py`) that asks a question this document
uniquely allows: the brief presents its evidence and its conclusion in the same
section, so *does the evidence shown carry the claim made?* That directly targets what
Codex said the problem was — *"the risk comes from the final inferential step"*.

It ran over 145 bolded claims in 8.8 s. It did not work well enough to use:

| | |
|---|---|
| supported | 12 |
| **review** | **113 (78%)** |
| unsupported | 4 |
| overstated | 16 |

And on the three claims that are known to be wrong:

| known misquote | Jev's top choice | confidence | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "roughly half of true pitch volume is invisible" | `overstates` | 0.27 | review |
| "the cocked position roughly **doubles** scalene stiffness" | `overstates` | 0.50 | review |
| "LE screening predicted 49.9% of shoulder distraction variance" | `says_nothing` | 0.44 | review |

**The direction is right on two of three and the confidence is nowhere near usable.**
All three land in `review`, where they are indistinguishable from 113 others.

### Why, and it is structural rather than a tuning problem

Look at what those two errors actually are. Takaba measured **14.4 vs 9.4 kPa**; the
brief calls that *"roughly doubles"*. It is 53%. Kamarajugadda measured **51.2% of
outings exceeding a recommendation**; the brief calls that *"roughly half of true pitch
volume"*. Both numbers are real, correctly transcribed, and sitting in the same
section as the claim.

That puts this class of error **between both mechanisms**:

- the **string match** passes, because every figure is present and correct;
- the **model** is being asked whether 14.4 against 9.4 is "roughly double", which is
  arithmetic — the one thing the jaggedness page says Jev is unreliable at, and the
  reason numbers were routed away from it in the first place.

A correct number, correctly quoted, wrongly characterised in words is the gap. Lowering
`AUTO_ACCEPT` does not close it: at a floor low enough to surface `overstates` at 0.27,
the 113 review items become 113 assertions and the tool is worse than nothing.

**What would close it** is a third mechanism, in code: extract (figure, characterising
word) pairs — "doubles", "roughly half", "an order of magnitude", "most" — and check
the arithmetic. 14.4/9.4 = 1.53, which is not "doubles"; that is a two-line comparison
once the pair is extracted, and it needs no model. That is the honest next build, and
it is a better use of effort than tuning a threshold.

### Smaller thing fixed on the way

Three of the four question-shaped lines in the brief came back flagged — the "Open
questions worth answering locally" section is entirely questions. Exactly the category
error already fixed in the deck verifier for `did.question`, not ported across.
Questions are now skipped here too, which is why the claim count is 145 rather than 149.

## Next

- **Build the figure-versus-characterisation check.** The TOS run above says this is
  where the real gap is: a correct number described in words the arithmetic does not
  support. It is a code check, not a model one, and it needs no new API surface.
- **Import the four TOS source papers** (`verifier/tos_sources/README.md`) so the brief
  can be checked against its sources rather than only against itself. Needs Eric: the
  bridge key is read-only.
- **Tune `AUTO_ACCEPT` against hand labels**, rather than leaving it at the cookbook's
  starting value.
- **Wire it into the Research in 5 workflow** so a deck cannot be published without
  passing. It is a CLI that exits non-zero for exactly this reason, but nothing calls
  it yet — `build.js` or the `/research-in-5` skill is the hook point.
- Then the status report, which needs reading first: if its fields name athletes or
  injuries, that content is tier B or C and cannot go to a cloud API as it stands.
